Transcript:
[00:00] Ava Martinez: hey everyone thanks for taking the time, um this is Ava from Redwood, i'm here with Samir and Jordan. Our goal is to walk through the private vpc networking assumptions and how that interacts with runtime performance, any initial constraints on your side maya?
[00:18] Maya Chen: yeah thanks, so quick background we are building a document generation and risk-scoring pipeline, low latency front-end for traders, so p99 is pretty important for us, target sub-250ms for short prompts, we have strict egress rules, all outbound must go through a corporate NAT and we prefer private connectivity where possible.
[00:40] Samir Patel: got it, thanks. Quick clarifying q: when you say corporate NAT, is that a centralized egress for the whole VPC or per-subnet nat gateways?
[00:50] Evan Brooks: currently centralized via a transit VPC, so traffic from our app subnets hits a transit stack which does egress, we try to avoid routes that leave the transit path, also we have dedicated AZs for compute.
[01:05] Jordan Lee: okay that makes sense. a few high-level patterns we see: 1) PrivateLink (interface endpoints) to the Redwood control plane + model registry, 2) a private dataplane option where inference nodes run inside your subnets and egress only to your on-prem data stores, and 3) hybrid where control-plane talks over PrivateLink but inference pops out via NAT for model artifact pulls — each has different latency/throughput and security tradeoffs.
[01:32] Priya Singh: can you expand on private data plane? Are we hosting inference on our own machines or is it dedicated instances in our VPC managed by Redwood?
[01:40] Ava Martinez: great question. Private deployment means the inference runtime runs on instances inside your VPC (Redwood VMs/AMI or our container images on your k8s). Redwood's control plane talks to agents via PrivateLink / interface endpoint so credentials never traverse public net. The runtime makes inference calls locally.
[01:57] Samir Patel: to add: if you go fully private, model weights and KV caches are local to your infra—so you remove cross-region transfer for kv cache lookups but you are responsible for placement and AZ traffic patterns which can affect p99.
[02:12] Maya Chen: right, so KV cache locality — if we have multi-AZ nodes and requests route to different AZs, can that cause KV cache misses and increase latency?
[02:22] Samir Patel: yes, exactly. If KV cache is shard-local or per-host, cross-AZ requests that hit a node without warmed KV will see cold start cost. Two patterns: 1) sticky routing so client requests for a conversation stick to the same backend, or 2) global KV sync—either via a fast in-VPC replication (redis/replication) or by pre-warming KV caches during deployment. Each has cost/complexity tradeoffs.
[02:45] Evan Brooks: sticky routing sounds appealing but we also have autoscaling — what happens when nodes terminate?
[02:52] Jordan Lee: autoscale churn is a challenge; we recommend a combination: proactive cache warmup hooks plus short-lived sticky sessions with fallback. For autoscale termination we have graceful drain hooks to snapshot KV or ensure the next node gets the warmed prefix. We also expose a warmup API for prefetching common prompts.
[03:10] Maya Chen: warmup API — can you share an example?
[03:14] Samir Patel: sure, it's a call to /v1/warmup with a set of prompt prefixes and expected sequence lengths; runtime will fetch tokenizer + prefix kv entries and load them into the KV store. We'll share the runbook.
[03:27] Priya Singh: on the networking side, PrivateLink is attractive because it avoids public egress, but we worry about interface endpoint scalability and per-AZ endpoints. Thoughts?
[03:36] Jordan Lee: PrivateLink requires an interface endpoint per AZ for best latency. You can front it with NLB inside Redwood side; still, traffic remains in the AWS backbone. For high throughput you might provision endpoints in each AZ where inference nodes live. If you can't deploy per-AZ, you will pay cross-AZ charges and see higher latency.
[03:56] Evan Brooks: do we need a NAT at all if we use PrivateLink for control plane? Our artifacts are in s3 — how does model weight pull work?
[04:04] Samir Patel: artifact pulls typically happen from our artifact repository. Options: 1) we push model blobs to your S3 bucket at onboarding via S3 replication (no outbound), 2) node pulls from external s3 via NAT — if that's not allowed we'd recommend pre-stage weights into your internal storage or allow Redwood access via VPC endpoint to our artifact store. We also support signed urls via PrivateLink to avoid public NAT egress.
[04:31] Maya Chen: okay good. latency wise, what's the delta between PrivateLink in same AZ vs cross-AZ NAT egress? ballpark numbers?
[04:41] Samir Patel: in our benchmarks, same-AZ PrivateLink adds ~2-8ms compared to local loopback, cross-AZ PrivateLink + charges add ~10-20ms, cross-AZ NAT egress to public endpoints can add 40–100ms depending on route. For p99-sensitive workloads we push for per-AZ endpoints and colocated inference capacity.
[05:02] Jordan Lee: also batching changes the story: small batch sizes (1-4) minimize latency but reduce throughput efficiency; larger batches increase throughput but can push p99 up. With quantized models you can often increase batch size without linear latency increase because compute per token decreases, but KV cache misses still dominate p99.
[05:22] Priya Singh: quantify 'quantized models' — are we talking int8 or other formats? How does that affect throughput and memory so we can place nodes appropriately?
[05:31] Samir Patel: we recommend int8/llm.int8 for many transformer models — you get 2–3x throughput improvement and 30–50% memory reduction. There are tradeoffs in quality; we test via Redwood Optimize profiles. On machine sizing this means you can host more replicas per GPU, but warmup time for kv cache is still needed.
[05:53] Maya Chen: what about CPU overhead for PrivateLink agents—do we need beefy control plane instances?
[05:58] Jordan Lee: control plane agents are lightweight; the heavy work is inference runtime on GPUs. The agent manages orchestration and health checks, a t3.medium equivalent is fine for control agents typically.
[06:10] Evan Brooks: we have strict DNS policies — internal private hosted zones only, no external recursion. Will your recommended PrivateLink require changes to our private DNS?
[06:19] Ava Martinez: on AWS we recommend using interface endpoints with private DNS enabled, which creates a vpc zone entry for the redwood service name. If you can't use private DNS, you can use explicit endpoint IPs in a config. We'll send a diagram showing the DNS resolution patterns.
[06:33] Priya Singh: what about health checks and control-plane telemetry, do logs go out over PrivateLink? We need audit logs in our SIEM.
[06:41] Jordan Lee: yes, control-plane telemetry can be routed over PrivateLink; we also support pushing logs to your Kinesis/CloudWatch via cross-account role or to a S3 bucket in your account. For audit logs we can provide syslog/s3 exports and the raw request traces for compliance.
[06:58] Maya Chen: let's talk KV cache specifics — if we colocate cache in-memory per replica, what's strategy for long-running conversations vs short stateless calls?
[07:08] Samir Patel: for long-running convos we do sticky routing so the conversation stays on a warmed replica. For many short stateless calls, prefix caching helps: common prefixes are replicated to all nodes at startup. For very heavy state we recommend a shared in-vpc redis as KV backing, but that introduces network hop latency. In tests shared redis added 5–15ms depending on AZ placement.
[07:33] Evan Brooks: is there an option for local in-memory KV with background async replication to other nodes?
[07:38] Jordan Lee: yes, eventual consistency async replication is our recommended compromise: the requester gets low-latency local hits while replication pushes updates to other nodes for subsequent requests. In practice this reduces p50 cost and keeps p99 bounded if requests are mostly localized.
[07:52] Maya Chen: for our use-case traders switch contexts a lot, so locality might be low. We probably need a shared redis or sticky routing and a client affinity layer. How much does a shared redis cost at our scale?
[08:03] Samir Patel: cost depends on throughput; given your QPS numbers, our rough estimate is X (we'll send a spreadsheet). But remember the redis latency tax — design for hot keys in-memory and cold keys via shared store.
[08:15] Ava Martinez: we'll attach the benchmark spreadsheet with cost numbers and a few scenarios.
[08:20] Priya Singh: about batching: you mentioned batching windows — can we tune batch timeouts to keep p99 under 250ms?
[08:27] Samir Patel: yes, runtime has adaptive batching: it starts a batch window (configurable, e.g., 10–50ms) and flushes early if latency SLO is close. For your target, we'd recommend a 10–15ms batch window with a max batch size of 8 for small prompts, combined with quantized models to keep compute <100ms. The key is to measure end-to-end: network + KV + compute + tokenization.
[08:51] Evan Brooks: tokenization overhead — is that done on the client or runtime?
[08:55] Jordan Lee: runtime handles tokenization by default, but you can pre-tokenize on the client to save time; however pre-tokenization affects cache keys, so you need consistent tokenization across clients. We recommend server-side tokenization unless you control all clients.
[09:10] Maya Chen: let's get concrete — can you walk us through a 1-request timeline and where ms are spent?
[09:15] Samir Patel: sure: 1) client request enters your LB -> hits an inference node (0–5ms intra-AZ), 2) tokenization (2–6ms), 3) KV cache lookup local (0–5ms) or remote (5–20ms), 4) batching wait (0–15ms depending), 5) compute (model dependent: 30–150ms), 6) response serialization and return (2–8ms). So p99 often dominated by compute + remote KV + cross-AZ network.
[09:43] Priya Singh: do you have any mitigations for cross-AZ network blips?
[09:46] Jordan Lee: we recommend AZ isolation for inference pods and per-AZ endpoints for control plane. Also, deploy smarts in the routing layer to prefer same-AZ nodes and fallback only when needed. Use health checks and circuit breakers to avoid routing to degraded AZs.
[09:59] Maya Chen: is there any observable we can surface in our console for kv hit rates and warmup?
[10:04] Samir Patel: yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-model p50/p95/p99, kv hit/miss metrics, average batch size, and per-instance CPU/GPU utilization. We'll enable a dashboard for your pilot.
[10:16] Evan Brooks: about encryption and keys — can we manage keys in our KMS?
[10:20] Ava Martinez: absolutely, we integrate with customer-managed KMS for model artifact encryption and TLS termination. Keys stay in your account when you choose the private deployment option.
[10:29] Priya Singh: compliance — we need SOC2 docs and any penetration test reports.
[10:33] Ava Martinez: we'll share SOC2 + network hardening docs; Samir will send a security packet after the call.
[10:40] Samir Patel: notes on benchmarking — for the pilot we'll run three scenarios: 1) same-AZ PrivateLink, 2) cross-AZ PrivateLink, 3) NAT egress to artifact store, and collect p50/p95/p99, kv hit rate, avg batch size, and end-to-end token latency. We'll run synthetics and a small replay of real traffic.
[11:00] Maya Chen: timeline?
[11:03] Ava Martinez: we can spin the pilot next week if your infra permissions are ready — estimate 2–3 days to stage weights and run tests, then a 1-hour steady-state run to gather metrics.
[11:12] Evan Brooks: permissions: we'll need a deployment runbook and an IAM role for the agent, plus network artifacts.
[11:20] Priya Singh: i'll confirm the egress policy and try to open a PrivateLink endpoint CIDR for your IPs if needed.
[11:25] Jordan Lee: thanks. also one gotcha: DNS TTLs on private hosted zones can cause old endpoints to be cached; use low TTL during migration.
[11:33] Maya Chen: good to know.
[11:36] Ava Martinez: doing a quick recap, agreed: 1) Redwood to share network checklist + PrivateLink diagram + SOC2 docs, 2) Samir to run 3-scenario pilot and share benchmark sheet, 3) Aurelius to confirm egress constraints and provide a small infra sandbox. Any other open questions?
[11:52] Priya Singh: none from security, thanks.
[11:54] Maya Chen: no, looks good.
[11:56] Evan Brooks: one last question — what happens to model updates? If we push a model patch does KV cache rebuild cause big hiccups?
[12:02] Samir Patel: model updates can be rolled via canary with warmup to avoid cold cache impact; we support staged rollouts and traffic mirroring for validation. We also support automatic fallback to previous model version in case of regression.
[12:16] Ava Martinez: perfect. we'll follow up with calendar invites for the pilot and a security sync. Thanks everyone.
